title: Dissertation Supplement
text: These supplementary materials accompany my dissertation, What to Suspect When They’re Expecting: Abortion Ambiguity, Hindsight Bias, and Probable Cause Determinations in Pregnancy Loss Investigations After Dobbs.

title: Pilot Study 1 Supplement: Supplementary Analyses
text:
About this document
This part includes the supplementary analyses for Pilot Study 1. The Pilot Study 1 materials include the registered models and hypotheses, narrative-coding reliability checks, and exploratory analyses supporting Chapter 5.

title: Registered Analytic Models and Hypotheses
text:
Analytic Models.
I conducted all analyses in R (R Core Team, 2026). Each research question was tested with its own model. Chi-square tests of independence compared the content of the narratives across the four crime categories (RQ1) and across the four verdict conditions (RQ2). These tests covered the 67 automated features (i.e., the Phase 1 and Phase 2 codes), with the Benjamini–Hochberg correction applied across that family. The 14 holistic codes (i.e., the Phase 3 codes) are complete. However, all but one fell below the preregistered threshold for inter-rater reliability. I therefore used the holistic codes only in the analyses of mitigating and aggravating factors and mental states (H2a, H2b, H2c, and H3a), and I treat every result that rests on a holistic code as exploratory. I report Cramér’s V with a 95% confidence interval for each variable.
A within-subjects one-way ANOVA tested whether post-narrative severity ratings differed across the four crime categories (RQ3, H3b). Each participant gave four ratings, one for each crime category. I applied the Greenhouse–Geisser correction when sphericity was violated. I fit the ANOVA with the afex package, computed estimated marginal means and planned contrasts with emmeans (Lenth & Piaskowski, 2017), and computed effect sizes with the effectsize package. Registered planned contrasts and main effects were tested at α = .05 without adjustment. The one exception was the follow-up of interactions. I corrected the simple effects that probe the interaction of verdict condition and factor type (H2b) within that family. I used Tukey’s HSD when the follow-up compared all pairs of estimated marginal means and the Bonferroni correction when it tested a specified subset.
Two multiple regressions tested whether scores on the Modified Abortion Attitudes Scale predicted each participant’s mean severity and mean punishment ratings across the four crime categories (RQ4, H4). Age, political orientation, and religiosity were covariates. I compared the card-sort consensus with the preregistered threshold descriptively (RQ5). Mixed-effects logistic regressions tested whether the features of each scenario predicted the binary judgment that the scenario was “definitely yes, this is a crime” (H5). Each model had a random intercept for participants. I fit these models with the lme4 and lmerTest packages. A pooled McNemar’s test across the 20 scenarios compared descriptive and normative crime judgments (RQ6, H6). The legal-accuracy analysis used one-sample binomial tests against chance (.50), for each scenario and pooled across scenarios. I computed the McNemar and exact binomial tests with the exact2x2 package. Two mixed-effects logistic regressions of the card-sort crime judgments tested the attitude hypotheses (RQ7, H7a and H7b). The first model pooled the two judgment types. The second added the interaction of abortion attitudes and judgment type. Both models had crossed random intercepts for participants and scenarios, and both were fit with lme4 and lmerTest.
I report effect sizes (i.e., partial \(\eta^2\), Cramér’s V, and odds ratios) and 95% confidence intervals for all tests. The cluster analysis is exploratory. It used partitioning around medoids on Gower distance within each crime category. I fit it with the cluster package and evaluated it with the silhouette width and the gap statistic. I computed scale descriptives and reliability coefficients with the psych package. The text analyses of the narratives used quanteda (Benoit et al., 2018), with quanteda.textstats and quanteda.textplots for keyness and text statistics and udpipe for linguistic annotation. I computed inter-rater reliability (i.e., Cohen’s and Fleiss’s kappa) with the irr package.
The two kinds of mixed-effects logistic regression take the following multilevel form. In the feature-prediction models (H5), crime judgments \(i\) are nested within participants \(j\). Each scenario feature \(F\) enters as a single Level-1 predictor:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Level 1:} \quad & \mathrm{logit}\big(\mathrm{Pr}(\text{crime}_{ij} = 1)\big) = \beta_{0j} + \beta_{1}\,F_{ij} \\
\text{Level 2:} \quad & \beta_{0j} = \gamma_{00} + u_{0j}, \quad u_{0j} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ \tau^{2}_{\text{participant}}).
\end{aligned}
\]
The attitude models (H7a and H7b) cross each judgment with both participants \(j\) and scenarios \(k\). Standardized abortion attitudes (\(\text{AAS}_j\)) enter as a participant-level (Level-2) predictor, and judgment type (descriptive vs. normative) enters as a Level-1 predictor:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Level 1:} \quad & \mathrm{logit}\big(\mathrm{Pr}(\text{crime}_{ijk} = 1)\big) = \beta_{0jk} + \beta_{1jk}\,\text{JudgmentType}_{ijk} \\
\text{Level 2:} \quad & \beta_{0jk} = \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01}\,\text{AAS}_{j} + u_{0j} + v_{0k} \\
& \beta_{1jk} = \gamma_{10} + \gamma_{11}\,\text{AAS}_{j} \\
& u_{0j} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ \tau^{2}_{\text{participant}}), \quad v_{0k} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ \tau^{2}_{\text{scenario}}).
\end{aligned}
\]
H7b tests whether the association between abortion attitudes and crime judgments differs by judgment type (\(\gamma_{11}\)). H7a tests the main-effects model, in which \(\gamma_{11} = 0\).

title: Pilot 1 Supplementary Analyses
text:
Validation and Reliability of the Narrative Coding
This section reports the checks on the narrative coding, the reliability of the holistic codes, the distributions of the ratings, the pairwise comparisons of the crime categories, and the exploratory analyses. Chapter 5 reports the main descriptive statistics, reliabilities, and results for each research question.
The narrative codes were assigned in three phases. In the first two phases, automated coding accepted a code when its certainty met a calibrated cutoff. Codes below the cutoff went to human coders in Phase 3. Table P1.2 shows the cutoff for each phase, and Table P1.3 shows the inter-rater reliability of the holistic Phase 3 codes. The keyness analyses in Table P1.4 and Table P1.5 serve as a convergent check on the coding. They show the words that most set each crime category apart from the others.
r
cert_tbl <- p1_cert |>
  mutate(
    phase     = stringr::str_to_title(phase),
    cutoff    = sprintf("%.2f", cutoff),
    precision = sprintf("%.2f", precision),
    recall    = sprintf("%.2f", recall),
    f1        = sprintf("%.2f", f1)
  ) |>
  select(phase, cutoff, n_accepted, n_routed, precision, recall, f1)

cert_tbl <- cert_tbl |> dplyr::rename(
  `Phase` = phase,
  `Cutoff` = cutoff,
  `n accepted` = n_accepted,
  `n routed` = n_routed,
  `Precision` = precision,
  `Recall` = recall,
  `F1` = f1
)

Levin, J. R., Serlin, R. C., & Seaman, M. A. (1994). A controlled, powerful multiple-comparison strategy for several situations. Psychological Bulletin, 115(1), 153–159. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.115.1.153

title: Verdicts, Mental State and Legal Accuracy
text:
Narrative Features by Verdict Condition (RQ2)
This chapter reports the analyses of the narratives by verdict condition (RQ2, H2a, H2b, and H2c) and three exploratory analyses. These are the accuracy of participants’ legal judgments, the three-way interaction of abortion attitudes, state law, and judgment type, and the comparison of the narratives with television plotlines and documented cases.
A series of descriptive chi-square tests compared the frequency of each feature across the four verdict conditions, with the Benjamini–Hochberg correction applied across the testable features (RQ2; see Table P1.10). After the correction, 12 features varied with the verdict participants were instructed to write toward, including legal terminology (\(\chi^2(3, N = 311) = 28.98\), BH-adjusted p < .001) and causal structure (V = .29).
r
rq2_tbl <- p1_rq2 |>
  arrange(p_bh, p) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  mutate(
    chisq      = sprintf("%.2f", chisq),
    cramers_v  = paste0(sub("^0", "", zr_fmt(cramers_v, 2)),
                        ifelse(is.na(p_bh), "",
                          ifelse(p_bh < .001, "***",
                          ifelse(p_bh < .01, "**",
                          ifelse(p_bh < .05, "*", ""))))),
    cv_ci      = gsub("\\b0\\.", ".", sprintf("[%s, %s]", zr_fmt(cv_ci_low, 2), zr_fmt(cv_ci_high, 2))),
    p_bh_fmt   = ifelse(p_bh < .001, "< .001",
                        sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p_bh)))
  ) |>
  select(variable, n, chisq, df, cramers_v, cv_ci, p_bh_fmt)

names(rq2_tbl) <- c("Variable", "n", "chi-square", "df", "Cramer's V", "95% CI", "p (BH)")

rq2_note <- paste0(
  "Chi-square tests of independence between verdict condition (4 levels) and each ",
  "narrative feature. n = number of narratives with the feature coded; Cramer's V is ",
  "reported with its 95% CI. p (BH) = p-value Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted across the ",
  "", sum(!is.na(p1_rq2$p_bh)), " testable Phase 1/2 features; the table lists the 10 features with the smallest adjusted p values. ",
  "Asterisks denote BH-adjusted significance: ",

title: Verdicts, Mental State and Legal Accuracy
text:
Mental State by Actual Culpability (H2c)
H2c rests on the coded mental-state category, so I report it as exploratory. H2c predicted that narratives in the culpable conditions would attribute purposeful or knowing mental states more often than narratives in the non-culpable conditions. The relationship between actual culpability and coded mental state was not significant, \(\chi^2\)(1, N = 279) = 0.32, p = .572. Contrary to H2c, coded mental state did not differ by actual culpability. However, the mental-state code did not meet the preregistered reliability target (ICC = .67, registered \(\kappa\) = .43, target = .80; see Table P1.3), leaving this result inconclusive. The code was not reliable enough to tell whether participants matched the mental state to the verdict they wrote toward or to the facts of the case.
crumbs: 4  Verdicts, Mental State and Legal Accuracy

title: Verdicts, Mental State and Legal Accuracy
section: Legal Accuracy of the Crime Judgments
text:
Legal Accuracy of the Crime Judgments
State-law coding. For the legal-accuracy sub-analysis, participants’ descriptive judgments (“Is this a crime where you live?”) were compared with the legal status of each scenario in their state of residence as of May 2026. Participant responses were matched based on accuracy (yes/no). However, given that the specifics of state laws regarding abortion remain in flux and convoluted, I did not interpret a mismatch as true ignorance of the underlying state-specific status. For example, many state abortion bans do not apply to pregnant people as a matter of black letter law, but they still can be, and have been, used to criminalize abortion (Weigel et al., 2020), so whether self-managed abortion is a crime in a given state is not a clear binary. Appendix A of the dissertation gives the coding rules and sources for each state and the confidence flags used in the preregistered sensitivity analysis.
I report the legal-accuracy analysis as exploratory. Compared with the state-law coding, accuracy differed significantly from chance on 19 of the 20 scenarios. Accuracy on the nine state-invariant scenarios ranged from .95 to 1.00 (M = .98) and was lower on the six abortion scenarios with between-state variance (.64 to .82, M = .76). The per-scenario accuracy tallies appear in Table P1.9.
crumbs: 4  Verdicts, Mental State and Legal Accuracy

title: Verdicts, Mental State and Legal Accuracy
section: Abortion Attitudes, State Law, and Judgment Type
text:
Abortion Attitudes, State Law, and Judgment Type
I report this analysis as exploratory. When the state-law coding was added to the mixed-effects model of card-sort crime judgments, the three-way Attitudes × State Law × Judgment Type interaction was significant (OR = 0.28, 95% CI [0.13, 0.63], z = −3.09, p = .002; see Table P1.7). Because Pilot 1 was not powered to detect three-way interactions (N = 81), I report this estimate descriptively.

title: Verdicts, Mental State and Legal Accuracy
section: Narratives Compared With Television Plotlines and Documented Cases
text:
Narratives Compared With Television Plotlines and Documented Cases
I report these comparisons as exploratory and descriptive. None was tested inferentially. As registered, I compared the abortion methods named in the narratives (i.e., the Section F method code) with the methods shown in U.S. television abortion plotlines (Herold & Sisson, 2019). I mapped the television categories onto the method code (see Table P1.11). The largest difference was for physical or instrument methods. They were named in .42 of the narratives that specified a method and in .67 of the procedures in the television plotlines.
The Section J code identified narratives referring to real-world cases. None of the 311 narratives referred to a documented real-world case. For the prosecution comparison, I used documented U.S. pregnancy-criminalization cases (Pregnancy Justice, 2023) in place of the registered television reference, which contains no account of actual prosecutions. I recorded this source change as a deviation. I prompted approximately .25 of the narratives for each crime category; these shares reflect the design rather than participants’ expectations. In documented prosecutions, charges for chemical endangerment (i.e., criminal child neglect, abuse, or endangerment) made up .84 of charged cases. Fetal homicide made up .06, improper disposal .03, and self-managed abortion .01. The balanced design therefore over-samples the three categories that are rare in actual prosecutions.

title: Pilot Study 2 Supplement: Full Analyses
text:
About this document
This part includes the full analyses for Pilot Study 2. Chapter 5 of the dissertation reports the hypotheses and main results. Here I report the analytic framework and hypotheses, the full results with their tables and figures, and the supplementary, exploratory, and robustness analyses.
The last chapter of this part (Simulation and Planning Outputs) includes simulation and planning outputs from before I analyzed the Pilot 2 data. I used the simulated estimates to plan the analyses; they do not describe the responses of Pilot 2 participants.

title: Analytic Framework and Hypotheses
text:
Analytic Framework.
I conducted all analyses in R (R Core Team, 2026). I estimated the hindsight effects with Bayesian multilevel models fit with the brms package (Bürkner, 2017, 2018) through the cmdstanr interface to Stan. Each participant received one kind of search outcome across the three vignettes and rated each vignette before and after learning its outcome. I accounted for these repeated ratings in the expected-versus-unexpected evidence comparison. I used non-criminal miscarriage as the reference case. I computed planned contrasts and average comparisons with marginaleffects (Arel-Bundock et al., 2024). I tested the mediation hypotheses with their indirect effects, which I summarized from the posterior draws with the posterior and bayestestR packages (Falk et al., 2023; Makowski et al., 2019; Miočević et al., 2018; Vuorre & Bolger, 2018). I based each conclusion on whether the 95% credible interval excluded zero (Kruschke & Liddell, 2018).
The preregistration allowed frequentist mixed factorial ANOVAs of the continuous outcomes. The analysis plan also included a GEE check of search-target endorsement. I evaluated the registered hypotheses with the Bayesian decision rules. This supplement reports the Bayesian results.
The multilevel models take the following form. \(Y\) is a continuous outcome measured on occasion \(t\) (i.e., before or after the outcome, or the vignette) within participant \(j\). The kind of incriminating evidence found, \(\text{Outcome}_j\), varies between participants:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Level 1:} \quad & Y_{tj} = \pi_{0j} + \pi_{1j}\,W_{tj} + e_{tj}, \quad e_{tj} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ \sigma^{2}) \\
\text{Level 2:} \quad & \pi_{0j} = \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01}\,\text{Outcome}_{j} + u_{0j} \\
& \pi_{1j} = \gamma_{10} + \gamma_{11}\,\text{Outcome}_{j} + u_{1j} \\
& (u_{0j},\ u_{1j})^{\top} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\ \mathbf{T}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(W_{tj}\) is the within-participant factor (i.e., before or after the outcome, or the vignette). The within-participant change is represented by \(\gamma_{10}\), with \(\gamma_{11}\) representing how that change depends on the kind of evidence found. Participant intercepts and slopes have covariance matrix \(\mathbf{T}\). For binary search-target endorsement, I retained the Level-2 structure and modeled \(\mathrm{logit}\big(\mathrm{Pr}(Y_{tj} = 1)\big)\) in place of \(Y_{tj}\), without a Level-1 residual term.
I used mean-zero Normal priors for the regression coefficients, with widths matched to the outcome scales to provide weak regularization. The log-odds coefficients of the binary-choice models had a similarly weak prior (Bürkner, 2018; Gelman et al., 2008; Gelman et al., 2014; Hox et al., 2018; Sorensen et al., 2016). I used an LKJ(2) prior for correlations among participant random effects and retained the scale-aware Student-t defaults in brms for intercepts, random-effect standard deviations, and residual standard deviations (Bürkner, 2017, 2018). For the H5a sensitivity check, I refit the model with half and twice the coefficient-prior widths (Depaoli et al., 2020; Hox et al., 2018). Appendix G of the dissertation records the priors and sampler settings.

title: Registered Analyses Reported in the Supplement
text:
Content Match: Subjective Probability of Guilt (H2a)
Of the three registered predictions reported here, H2a concerned whether guilt-probability ratings changed more after expected than unexpected evidence, particularly in the two criminal-conduct scenarios. I expected the narrative-prototype ordering of the scenarios to hold for pregnancy-specific likelihood changes after expected evidence (H2c), and the Model Penal Code culpability hierarchy to hold for mental-state ratings within each evidence condition (H5d). None of the three predictions met all registered support criteria.
For the observed means and standard deviations, I averaged each participant’s ratings over the three scenarios. Model estimates are posterior medians with 95% HDIs; probability of direction (pd) is the proportion of draws with the median’s sign. Differences in likelihood and guilt probability retain the 0–100 units.
I predicted that, after expected incriminating evidence, participants would inflate the subjective probability of the suspect’s guilt relative to their own pre-search ratings, more so than after unexpected incriminating evidence, and more so in the self-managed abortion and criminal miscarriage scenarios than in the non-criminal miscarriage scenario (H2a).
Consistent with the first part of H2a, the change in the subjective probability of the suspect’s guilt from before to after the search outcome was larger after expected than after unexpected incriminating evidence (16.49, 95% HDI [12.60, 20.47], pd > 99.9%). After expected incriminating evidence, ratings rose from before the search outcome (M = 61.16, SD = 22.26) to after it (M = 69.83, SD = 22.81), an estimated change of 8.55, 95% HDI [5.70, 11.36]; after unexpected incriminating evidence, they fell (before: M = 62.55, SD = 24.10; after: M = 54.50, SD = 25.52), an estimated change of −7.94, 95% HDI [−10.73, −5.20]. Contrary to the second part of H2a, the increase after expected incriminating evidence was not reliably larger in the self-managed abortion and criminal miscarriage scenarios than in the non-criminal miscarriage scenario (posterior probability .103, below the registered threshold). Descriptively, it was largest in the non-criminal miscarriage scenario (10.90) and smaller in the self-managed abortion (8.60) and criminal miscarriage (6.16) scenarios.
Registered verdict. Not supported by all registered criteria.

title: Registered Analyses Reported in the Supplement
text:
Inevitability (H2c)
I further predicted that the change in the pregnancy-specific likelihood would follow the narrative-prototype pattern (criminal miscarriage > self-managed abortion > non-criminal miscarriage; H2c).
H2c predicted the largest increase in disposal or concealment likelihood in the criminal miscarriage scenario after expected incriminating evidence. However, its change did not credibly exceed zero (−0.81, 95% HDI [−5.75, 3.92], pd = 62.9%), nor did the changes in the other two scenarios, and the probability of the predicted ordering was below .001. The non-criminal miscarriage comparison also ran contrary to the prediction: the mean of the two pregnancy items increased (95% HDI [8.43, 15.16]).
Registered verdict. Not supported by all registered criteria. I checked convergence for all parameters and for the registered coefficients separately, using the criteria in Appendix G. The all-parameter check failed. Neither diagnostic reading supported H2c; a failed convergence criterion precludes registered support.

title: Registered Analyses Reported in the Supplement
text:
Mens Rea Hierarchy (H5d)
I predicted the Model Penal Code culpability ordering in participants’ mental-state ratings within each evidence condition (H5d).
H5d was not supported in either evidence condition. Participants gave higher ratings to purposely than to knowingly after expected incriminating evidence (0.13, 95% HDI [0.02, 0.25], pd = 98.7%). The purposely-minus-knowingly difference after unexpected incriminating evidence had a 95% HDI that included zero (−0.05, 95% HDI [−0.17, 0.06], pd = 82.4%). The 95% HDI of recklessly minus negligently included zero after expected incriminating evidence (−0.02, 95% HDI [−0.16, 0.11], pd = 63.8%) and lay below zero after unexpected incriminating evidence (−0.44, 95% HDI [−0.58, −0.31], pd > 99.9%). Participants rated recklessly above knowingly after expected (−0.21, 95% HDI [−0.36, −0.08], pd = 99.9%) and unexpected incriminating evidence (−0.45, 95% HDI [−0.58, −0.31], pd > 99.9%): both knowingly-minus-recklessly intervals lay below zero. This comparison is reported but is not a required part of the registered decision.
Registered verdict. Not supported by all registered criteria.

title: Evidence Reinterpretation (RQ3)
text:
RH1.4 was supported on the respecified item-level model (Table P2.23). The interaction of timing, outcome, and key consistency was 0.77, 95% HDI [0.52, 1.02], Pr(effect > 0) > .999, BF₁₀ > 1000. The 95% HDI meets the registered rule that it lie above zero. The model met the registered convergence criteria.
I respecified the model because the registered model nests item consistency within outcome. The respecified model codes each item, for every participant, by whether it would be consistent with the expected outcome. After inspecting the raw means, I chose to compare the same items across the randomly assigned outcomes. I made that choice before fitting the revised model. That timing makes the test less severe (see item 9.1 of the Pilot 2 deviations record on the study’s OSF page).
The registered model tests the interaction of timing and item consistency, with NCM as the reference vignette (Table P2.24). Its 95% HDI meets the registered criterion of a positive interval. Its registered convergence criteria were met (worst within-imputation R-hat = 1.002, lowest effective sample size = 2250, total divergent transitions = 0). In the eight-item sensitivity analysis without items 3 and 10, the result of the registered model holds (0.68 [0.49, 0.87]). The result of the respecified model does not hold (0.23 [−0.08, 0.54]). Without those two items, its key contrast rests on the NCM vignette alone (see item 9.2 of the deviations record). The change in the observed composite is descriptive. The exploratory tests for each item below keep the registered grouping by vignette.
The registered model had a divergent transition. To address it, I refit the model on the fourth imputed data set with adapt_delta = .99 (previously .95) and kept the other four fits. The model, priors, data, random seeds, initial values, and iteration counts did not change.

Predictive Checks for the H5a Model
This chapter reports the checks on the RH5.6 ordering and on the H5a model. They include the sensitivity of the H5a result to the priors and exclusions and the predictive checks of the model.

title: S1. Deviations from the registration
text:
Deviations
For each departure, I recorded when I chose it, whether I had seen the data, and the analytic discretion it allowed. Following Lakens (2024), I assessed test severity separately from the validity of the inference. Severity concerns how likely a test is to support a true hypothesis and to withhold support from a false one. A departure can leave severity unchanged, reduce it, or increase it; improving validity does not necessarily make a test more severe.
The five overlapping categories are unforeseen events, mistakes in the preregistration or study, missing information, violations of untested assumptions, and falsified auxiliary hypotheses. Each entry assesses severity, and entries involving a mistake, violated assumption, or falsified auxiliary hypothesis also assess validity. I retained the decision rules in the preregistration and its supplement.

title: S1. Deviations from the registration
text:
1. E4a Sensitivity Analysis
Registered on 2026-09-21. Added on 2026-09-25, while Study 1 data collection was under way and before any relevance rating had been analyzed.
What was registered. E4a concerns whether self-managed abortion (SMA) evidence increases the relevance of outcome-consistent items more than inconsistent items. Its parameter is the SMA × Consistency interaction in relevance ~ outcome × consistency + legal context + attitudes + (1 + consistency | participant) + (1 | item), with items 1, 6, and 7 coded consistent and the other seven coded inconsistent (analysis supplement, §E4a).
What I added. I reran E4a without the employment item (3) and the age and household item (10), using the same model and decision rule on the remaining eight items. The ten-item analysis remains the registered result; I report the sensitivity analysis beside it.
Why. In Pilot 2, items 3 and 10 received the lowest relevance ratings, changed little with the search outcome, and formed a separate background factor in every vignette. Study 1 largely retained the wording and consistency coding from the non-criminal miscarriage vignette, where both items were coded inconsistent. The E4a contrast could therefore partly compare information about the loss with background details. In that Pilot 2 vignette, the raw difference-in-differences was +0.87 with the background items and +0.50 without them (Pilot 2 deviations record, §9.2). I used the eight-item version to check E4a’s dependence on those items.
Category. Not a deviation. I added a sensitivity analysis based only on Pilot 2, before Study 1 data collection ended and before I saw any Study 1 relevance rating. The registered analysis and its severity are unchanged.

title: S1. Deviations from the registration
text:
2. Substitute Mediator (H3c–H3e)
Registered on 2026-09-21. Recorded on 2026-09-26, after Study 1 data collection ended and before any Study 1 outcome had been analyzed.
What was registered. H3c–H3e test whether outcome information relates to blame of the suspect indirectly, “through how likely participants think it is that the suspect committed the offense.” The indirect effect was predicted to be positive after SMA evidence (H3c) and negative after financial-crime evidence (H3d), each compared with no outcome information. H3e predicts a more positive indirect effect after SMA than financial-crime evidence. I specified separate groups for the two legal contexts, adjusting each equation for the four attitudes. Percentile 95% bootstrap intervals (10,000 samples) evaluate the indirect effects and their difference; robust Wald intervals describe the individual paths. The model is estimated again without the attitudes, and support is read on the indirect effects alone (analysis supplement, “Probability and blame (H3c–H3e)” and Figure 4). The registered mediator is a single item rated from 0 to 100: “Based on the evidence available at the time the warrant was sought, what is the probability that the suspect committed the crime the detective suspects her of committing?”
What happened. A technical glitch prevented the survey from displaying the probability-of-guilt question, leaving no responses to the registered mediator.
What the analysis does instead. I retained the H3c–H3e model, intervals, and decision rules but supplied pregnancy-evidence likelihood as the mediator. This registered 0–100 composite combines the likelihood ratings for abortion and disposal evidence and is also the mediator in E9a–E9b. S7 reports the analysis as a substitute. Chapter 5 reports H3a–H3b’s registered blame comparisons and explains in a footnote why H3c–H3e could not be tested as registered.
Why this measure. I chose pregnancy-evidence likelihood because a judgment that the search would uncover evidence of an offense bears on whether the suspect committed it, the relationship posited in H3c–H3e. Foreseeability measures predictability from the detective’s perspective; E9 specifies no directional prediction through it. Pregnancy-evidence likelihood addresses the related likelihood question, but it does not directly measure the probability of guilt.
Category. A mistake in the study: the survey omitted a registered item. I chose the existing pregnancy-evidence measure after data collection ended but before analyzing any Study 1 outcome or examining a likelihood or blame value. I considered no other candidate. With the registered mediator unavailable, I cannot assess the severity of that test. I report the substitute’s verdicts only for the related question it answers.

title: S1. Deviations from the registration
text:
3. Evidence-Relevance Structure
Registered on 2026-09-21. Recorded on 2026-10-01, after the Study 1 data had been analyzed.
What was registered. The measurement procedure chooses a factor structure for the ten relevance ratings with parallel analysis, a screen that requires at least three items per factor, and registered fit criteria. If no structure qualifies, the analyses use the ten-item mean. The procedure makes no provision for removing items. With more than one factor, each factor is a separate mediator, and the decision reads the sum across factors (analysis supplement, measurement and H1 sections).
What happened. No structure qualified, so every registered analysis uses the ten-item mean, and those results stand. The three-factor pattern failed the screen because its third factor had only two items. Both items described the suspect’s background. Item 3 said that she had held a stable job for several years, and item 10 said that she was 32 years old and lived with her husband.
What I added. Without items 3 and 10, the other eight items formed two factors. Items 1, 6, and 7 formed one factor, and items 2, 4, 5, 8, and 9 formed the other. This is the item-consistency key of E4a. I adopted this structure because of the content of the items, not by the registered rule, and it fails the registered fit criteria. I refit the six structural models that use the relevance mediator with this structure (H1a–H1d and E1a–E1b; H2a–H2b; E6a–E6f; E12a–E12d; H4b–H4d). These analyses applied the registered decision rules to the sum across factors, with 10,000 bootstrap attempts. I made no decision for E12a–E12c because fewer attempts were usable than the registration requires. These supplementary results accompany the registered results without replacing them. All Study 1 analyses used 10,000 bootstrap attempts, including this analysis.
Category. A violation of an untested assumption (i.e., that each indicated factor would have at least three qualifying items). I decided on this analysis after the data had been analyzed, so it tests the hypotheses less severely than the registered analysis.

title: S1. Deviations from the registration
text:
4. Relative Relevance (H1; H4b–H4d)
Registered on 2026-09-21. Decided on 2026-10-01, after the Study 1 data had been analyzed.
What was registered. H1 and H4b–H4d predict that outcome information changes the relevance of fitting evidence relative to non-fitting evidence. The structural models use evidence relevance as the mediator, which the registered measurement procedure made the ten-item mean (see item 3). Only E4a tests the relative item-level change directly, and that model has no likelihood outcome.
What the analysis does instead. In the Chapter 5 H1 and H4b–H4d analyses, I supplied relative relevance as the observed mediator: the mean for items consistent with self-managed abortion (i.e., items 1, 6, and 7, as coded for E4a) minus the mean for the remaining items. I used the ten-item key for the primary analysis and omitted background items 3 and 10 for the sensitivity analysis (see item 1). An added step supplied the mediator to the unchanged registered code. Models, samples, grouping and constraints, covariates, missing-data handling, the 10,000-attempt participant bootstrap, and decision rules remained as registered. Because the key codes fit to the self-managed abortion outcome only, relative relevance does not test sense-making after financial-crime evidence (H1b and H4c). The registered results based on the ten-item mean for all of these hypotheses, and the two-factor analysis from item 3, are reported in this supplement.
Why. The consistent-minus-inconsistent mean measures the relative change even when the mean across all ten items stays constant or falls.
Category. A mistake in the preregistration. I could have recognized the mismatch between the mean and the predicted quantity before collecting data, but chose the replacement only after seeing the registered results. This choice reduced the severity of the relative-relevance tests, although it improved construct validity. Their H1a–H1d and H4b–H4d decisions may differ from the registered decisions.

title: S1. Deviations from the registration
text:
5. Exploratory Suspect Judgments
Registered on 2026-09-21. Tests added on 2026-10-01, after I had seen the Study 1 results.
What was registered. H3a–H3b compare suspect blame across outcome conditions using an Outcome × Legal Context analysis of covariance; E7a–E7g use that model for punishment, recklessness, and negligence. E8b jointly models responsibility and the wrongness of the suspect’s conduct with blame and punishment, while the sample descriptions report that wrongness rating by condition (analysis supplement, “Sample descriptions and evidence measurement”). The registration provides no test of causality, preventability, favorable impression, justified reasons, wrongness apart from the law, wrongness given the charge, or counterfactual availability (study materials, sections H and I). Earlier E6a–E6c plans covered causality, preventability, and favorable impression but were withdrawn before registration.
What I added. After seeing the Study 1 results, I added tests on 2026-10-01 for nine judgments: causality, preventability, favorable impression, justified reasons, wrongness apart from the law, wrongness given the charge, counterfactual availability, the wrongness of the suspect’s conduct, and responsibility. I used the H3a–H3b blame model, substituting each judgment as the outcome. For each, I compared expected evidence with no information, unexpected evidence with no information, and expected with unexpected evidence, weighting the two legal contexts equally. The comparisons use Student t 95% intervals from the conventional covariance, with and without the four attitudes, in the analysis sample (N = 398) and registered sensitivity sample (N = 341). Although E8b includes responsibility and wrongness, its joint model gives normal Wald intervals; these additional tests give the blame model’s t intervals. The model with the registered covariates and sample adds 27 tests (i.e., nine judgments with three comparisons each), and the three companion versions add 81. I applied no multiplicity correction, consistent with the registered single-judgment comparisons.
Why. I added the pairwise comparisons to report judgments of the women consistently across studies.
Category. Not a deviation. These exploratory additions carry no letter or decision and do not alter any registered model, rule, test, or verdict. I chose them with the results in view, so their severity is low; the severity of the registered tests is unchanged.

Fitted two-mediator chains of confidence in the ruling (E13i–E13p)

Note. Fitted parallel mediation model of outcome information and confidence in the ruling in the primary sample, with likelihood and foreseeability as mediators and the four attitudes as covariates. The likelihood and foreseeability coefficients on confidence are E13i and E13j. title: Study 2 Supplement: Supplementary Tables and Figures
text:
About this document
This part includes the supplementary tables and figures for Study 2. For the main findings, see Chapter 5. The supplementary materials cover data cleaning and missing data, descriptive and preliminary analyses, manipulation checks, RQ1 through RQ5, and the sensitivity sample. Within S1 through S9, I grouped each analysis with its hypotheses and comparisons. The tables and figures reproduce the final Study 2 estimates.
For example, Table S4.1 begins S4. The H4a–H4h comparisons and adjusted H4 means are in S6.

Every comparison the analysis saves for the two ANCOVAs, in each of the four versions: the restricted-versus-full F, the within-evidence comparisons, the averaged comparisons (the stereotypicality-fallback secondary estimates), the baseline expectation and the between-evidence differences of each outcome effect. Adjusted versions control for the four attitude measures; unadjusted versions do not. Rows marked (reported), SMA − NCM within each evidence condition, are reported comparisons, not registered ones: the registration compares each outcome condition with no outcome information and treats every other comparison as exploratory, so they carry no letter, direction or decision. I added them after registration (2026-09-29), using the fitted models. Rows marked (reported) were added after registration and were tested with Fisher's protected least significant difference procedure; a comparison is significant only when the omnibus test of the three outcome conditions is significant (Levin et al., 1994). Omnibus test = the joint test that SMA − None and NCM − None within that evidence condition are both zero, F(2, residual df), from the same fit and coefficient covariance as the comparisons (not the restricted-versus-full F). Protected p = the larger of the comparison's own p and the omnibus p; a reported comparison is significant when its protected p is below .05. — = a saved row: the registration tests its comparisons without an omnibus gate. Tukey-adjusted p values are shown as a check on the procedure; the significance decisions follow the protected least significant difference procedure. Intervals: Student t with the residual df from the full coefficient covariance, 95% for every row except the two equivalence rows (H1b, H1g), which carry the registered 90% TOST interval. A threshold is unavailable when no crossing occurs, a curve crosses downward or more than once, or numerical calculations cannot resolve a crossing (registered analysis supplement); E4k has no registered decision rule, so an unavailable threshold changes no decision. Crossing = the rating on the 0–100 subjective-probability-of-guilt scale at which the average predicted probability of a yes ruling, over every included participant in their own evidence condition, reaches .50 under that outcome information (a single upward crossing; flat, decreasing, absent, multiple or unresolved crossings are unavailable). Both use the same participants and bootstrap draws; WLSMV probit, theta parameterization, four common attitude slopes in the adjusted versions. 95% CI = participant percentile bootstrap interval; the registration requires every required crossing in all 10,000 attempts. — = no interval: Threshold requires every attempt to be valid; Original target unavailable (usable attempts 3118 of 10000; 2345 of 10000; 961 of 10000; 6648 of 10000; 9261 of 10000; 6185 of 10000). Two-part award model: a logistic part for any award and a Gamma part with log link for the positive amount, each with six condition intercepts and six abortion-attitude slopes; plaintiff and officer blame and the other three attitudes carry slopes common to the six conditions, separately in each part; one Gamma dispersion. The last row subtracts the lower-score difference from the higher-score difference (registered analysis supplement). The 95% interval bounds the expected-award difference only: participant percentile bootstrap, refitting both parts and recomputing each attempt's own attitude mean and SD. The probability and positive-award differences are descriptive parts of the same predictions and carry no interval. E5b is registered without a direction and is reported without a support gate. Decision for E5b: estimates reported; no registered decision rule. Decision: each letter's registered rule applied to its saved interval.
